Lys2 A/PCP Is Covalently Loaded with [35S]S-Carboxymethylcysteine. The above demonstration that Lys2 A/PCP is both active for α-aminoadipate-AMP formation and covalently primable with phosphopantetheine on its PCP domain led us to the next experimental test of mechanism. After Lys2 has been phosphopantetheinylated, we propose that the Ppant terminal thiol attacks the aminoacyl adenylate, loading the amino acid onto Lys2 via a covalent thioester linkage to the holo-PCP domain (Figure 5B). The l-α-aminoadipate analogue [35S]S-carboxymethyl-l-cysteine, prepared by custom synthesis, was employed to detect this loading in a TCA precipitation assay. Loading was observed to be proportional to Lys2 A/PCP concentration and saturable over time (data not shown). In addition, aminoacylation was demonstrated to be CoASH-dependent, as visualized by SDS gel electrophoresis and autoradiography (Figure 5A), demonstrating radioactive 105-kDa Lys2 A/PCP double-domain-labeled with the [35S]S-CMCys.
Holo-Lys2 Produces α-Aminoadipate Semialdehyde. The formation of the product of reduction of α-aminoadipate, α-aminoadipate semialdehyde, can be monitored spectrophotometrically. From this assay, the Km of Lys2 for NADPH was determined to be 620 μM and the kcat for α-aminoadipate semialdehyde production to be 670 min-1 (Figure 6). Under identical conditions, but without CoASH, a low level of product was formed, presumably resulting from a small fraction of holo-Lys2 phosphopantetheinylated in vivo during overexpression in E. coli.
NADPH Addition Causes Cleavage of the [35S]S-Carboxymethylcysteine-S-Lys2 Acyl Enzyme. If the aminoacyl-S-PCP acyl enzyme (Figure 5B) is an intermediate in catalytic turnover, then it should be reductively released by the cosubstrate NADPH (Scheme 3). A TCA precipitation assay was employed to assess whether NADPH can reductively release thioesterified [35S]S-CMCys from Lys2. After preincubation with Lys5, holo-Lys2 rapidly accumulated the [35S]S-CMCys acyl-S-PCP intermediate in the absence of NADPH, as detectable by TCA precipitation (Figure 7). On addition of NADPH at the 180-s time point and TCA precipitation at 300 s, the 35S label was discharged, consistent with the reductive cleavage of the radioactive acyl-S-PCP form of Lys2 in the presence of NADPH.

Discussion
This study reveals the molecular logic of the two-protein system of S. cerevisiae Lys2 and Lys5, found in S. cerevisiae and other fungi that produce lysine via the fungal homocitrate/aminoadipate route. The large size of Lys2 (155 kDa) is a reflection of at least three and possibly four component domains (Figure 2). Residues 1−224 are presently unassigned for function, while residues 225−808 constitute a typical 60-kDa adenylation (A) domain for aminoacyl-AMP formation. Residues 809−924 comprise the apo-PCP domain and 925−1392 the NADPH-utilizing reductase domain. In this work, we have assessed elements of function of the A domain, PCP domain, and complete Lys2 enzyme.
The ability to express and overproduce the 14-kDa PCP domain in E. coli provided the initial substrate to assay and validate the catalytic posttranslational modification function of S. cerevisiae Lys5. Lys5, also overproduced in and purified from E. coli, displayed strong homology to PPTases, which load an apo-PCP domain with the phosphopantetheinyl moiety of CoASH ( 16). Both covalent incorporation of tritiated phosphopantetheine catalyzed by Lys5 and mass spectrometric analysis confirmed holo-Lys2 PCP domain formation. These results established Lys5 as priming enzyme for Lys2 and were then corroborated using the larger, two-domain fragment, Lys2 A/PCP.
Lys5 appears to exhibit specificity toward apo-PCP domain substrates (data not shown). While we have not assessed the ability of Lys5 to prime the apo-ACP domains of either the yeast cytoplasmic type I fatty acid synthase (FAS) or the mitochondrial apo-ACP of type II FAS, Stuible et al. have recently noted that knockouts of FAS2, PPT2, and Lys5 have specific and nonoverlapping phenotypes, consistent with partner protein-specific priming by these three yeast PPTases ( 24).
In turn, the primed, holo form of Lys2 A/PCP was then a proper substrate to evaluate the next step in the proposed mechanism, activation of the amino acid α-aminoadipate and transfer onto the phosphopantetheinyl terminal thiol as a covalent acyl-S-PCP enzyme intermediate. Because radiolabeled aminoadipate was not commercially available, to demonstrate covalent attachment to Lys2 A/PCP we sought a surrogate amino acid that was both available in radiolabeled form and a substrate for the A domain. The A domain is conveniently assayed by amino acid-dependent [32P]PPi/ATP exchange which revealed that S-carboxymethyl-l-cysteine, an analogue of aminoadipate with C4 replaced by sulfur, sustained a robust isotope exchange (Table 1). We then demonstrated formation of the acyl enzyme CMCys-S-Lys2 A/PCP using [35S]S-CMCys as a substrate, dependent on prior phosphopantetheinylation with Lys5.
We next expressed the full-length 155-kDa S. cerevisiae Lys2 in E. coli, purified it to homogeneity, and demonstrated its activity, formation of α-aminoadipate semialdehyde (kcat = 11 s-1). Finally, we validated that the radiolabeled CMCys-S-enzyme (and correspondingly the α-aminoadipoyl-S-enzyme in normal turnover) is reductively cleaved by NADPH. Thus the catalytic logic for Lys2 to produce the C6 aldehyde from C6 α-aminoadipate is to reduce not the free acid nor the acyl-AMP but rather an acyl-thioester, covalently tethered at the PCP domain (Scheme 1b). This has clear formal mechanistic analogy to the reverse direction of the well-known glycolytic enzyme glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH) ( 25). In the case of GAPDH, the three-carbon aldehyde substrate reacts with an active site thiol, provided by a cysteine side chain, to reversibly form the thiohemiacetal tetrahedral adduct. Now, oxidation yields the acyl enzyme thioester intermediate (Scheme 3). The acyl group is phosphorylated by Pi in the GAPDH case, by AMP in the Lys2 back reaction.
With regard to catalytic strategy of Lys2, why convert the acyl-AMP intermediate to the acyl-S-enzyme intermediate before reduction, or for that matter why spend an ATP and not just reduce the free acid? For both Lys2 and GAPDH, from a thermodynamic perspective, thiohemiacetals are much easier to oxidize than free aldehydes and also to reduce than free acids. The input of energy then is required to convert the resonance-stabilized COO- of substrates to activated derivatives (RCOO-AMP, RCOO-PO3) to accumulate to high mole fraction the RCOS-enzyme that reacts with hydride from reduced nicotinamide coenzyme.
The organization of Lys2 is unusual for a non-ribosomal peptide synthetase, with a reductase domain fused downstream of the prototypic A/PCP domain pair. In a formal sense, the reductase domain is the element catalyzing release of the covalent acyl-enzyme intermediate. In most NRPS and PKS multimodular enzyme systems, acyl chain release is believed to be catalyzed by a thioesterase (TE) domain ( 26, 27). The chain release is then generally hydrolytic with either water or an electron-rich internal group (e.g., a side chain −OH) in the acyl chain acting as the kinetically competent nucleophile to release the completed natural product as a free acid (e.g., vancomycin, ACV) ( 28, 29), cyclic lactone (e.g., erythromycin) ( 27), or cyclic lactam (e.g., bacitracin) ( 26). In the Lys2 case, hydrolytic release of the C6 aminoadipoyl-S-PCP-enzyme would be an energy-wasting futile cycle and hydrolysis is probably scrupulously avoided. Reductive release rather than hydrolytic release generates aldehyde rather than acid product. One does not expect reductive release to be the favored acyl enzyme chain cleavage route in the termination steps of most NRPS and PKS catalysts because, in general, free aldehydes are more thermodynamically activated and act as uncontrollably reactive carbonyl groups in biological milieus. In the Lys2 case, the α-aminoadipate semialdehyde cyclizes rapidly and essentially quantitatively to the cyclic imine, Δ1-piperidine carboxylate, suppressing adventitious reactivity.
Homology searches for other NRPS catalysts with reductase domains fused downstream of A/PCP paired domains turn up two additional examples, the saframycin biosynthetic system ( 9) and the nrp cluster in the Mycobacterium tuberculosis genome ( 30). The substrates and products of the mycobacterial nrp are as yet unknown, but in saframycin biosynthesis an Ala-Gly-Tyr-Tyr-CHO is likely to be reductively released by this route prior to intramolecular cyclization to a six-ring hemiaminal structure in the antitumor antibiotic ( 30).
A second unusual feature of Lys2 as a non-ribosomal peptide synthetase type catalyst is its regiospecific activation of its amino acid substrate. Activation of l-α-aminoadipate not at the α (C2) carboxylate but rather at the distal ε (C6) carboxylate results in a relaxed specificity toward the α carbon chirality, since d-α-aminoadipate is reversibly activated as the aminoacyl-AMP (Table 1) as is the desamino substrate adipate. In this regard, the adenylation domain of Lys2 behaves more like a fatty acid-activating domain than a typical amino acid-activating domain.
An analogous fungal α-aminoadipate-activating domain with specificity for AMP attachment at substrate C6 is ACV synthetase ( 5), which produces the penicillin precursor tripeptide l-δ-(α-aminoadipoyl)-cysteine-d-valine. As in Lys2, in ACV synthetase, the adenylation domain for l-α-aminoadipate is at the N-terminus of the first module and also activates S-carboxymethylcysteine. It is conceivable that the A domains of ACV synthetase and Lys2 are exchangeable. The A domain of Lys2 may be prototypic for activation and incorporation of nonproteinogenic β and γ amino acids by many NRPSs to create nonstandard peptide connectivity, for example, the β-alanyl residues in the antitumor antibiotic bleomycin ( 31).
With the molecular logic of Lys2 revealed as an NRPS with a reductase domain fused in frame and of Lys5 as a priming PPTase, this information may be useful for design of inhibitors as antifungal agents since Lys2 and Lys5 are essential for fungal growth ( 12). Indeed, the recent sequencing of the LYS2 homologue from the human pathogen C. albicans ( 8) reveals it has the same domain organization as S. cerevisiae Lys2.

Reaction mechanism of Zn2+-dependent d-serine dehydratase: role of a conserved tyrosine residue interacting with pyridine ring nitrogen of pyridoxal 5′-phosphate

d-Serine dehydratase from Saccharomyces cerevisiae (Dsd1p) is a pyridoxal 5′-phosphate (PLP)- and Zn2+-dependent enzyme that catalyzes the dehydration of d-serine to yield pyruvate and ammonia. Dsd1p uses the Tyr residue (Y203) to interact with the pyridine nitrogen of PLP, which is a unique feature of PLP enzymes. To investigate the role of Y203 in catalysis, a series of Y203 mutants was constructed and studied. Mutant enzymes possessing a non-polar or a basic residue instead of Y203 (Y203F, A, S and R) exhibited substantial levels of catalytic activity, and among these, the Y203F mutant had the least impact on catalytic activity. The Y203D exhibited a 105-fold decrease in enzyme activity, and unlike wild-type enzyme, the mutant enzyme favoured the Cα reprotonation before hydroxyl group protonation. Our data show that the Y203 does not participate in the protonation of the pyridine nitrogen (N1) of PLP, and Dsd1p uses the cofactor in an N1-unprotonated state. The unprotonated N1 promotes elimination of the leaving group and evades Cα reprotonation before hydroxyl group protonation.

d-Serine dehydratase catalyzes the deamination of d-serine to yield pyruvate and ammonia using pyridoxal 5′-phosphate (PLP) as a cofactor. To date, two types of PLP-dependent d-serine dehydratase have been identified. One type is the enzyme belonging to the fold-type II PLP-dependent enzyme, and the representative enzyme is DsdA of Escherichia coli (1–4). The other type of enzyme is the fold-type III PLP-dependent enzyme. We previously identified the first fold-type III d-serine dehydratase (Dsd1p) from the budding yeast, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, and demonstrated that the enzyme requires a Zn2+, in addition to PLP (5, 6). Tanaka et al. also identified a fold-type III d-serine dehydratase from chicken kidney (chDsd) (7), which has been recently shown to be Zn2+-dependent (8). Except for mammals, fold-type III d-serine dehydratases are widely distributed in various eukaryotic organisms such as yeasts, birds, fishes and molds, as well as in various bacterial species. We believe that the Zn2+ requirement is the main characteristic feature of the fold-type III d-serine dehydratases. We have overexpressed and examined three Dsd1p homologs in Schizosaccharomyces pombe, Dictyostelium discoideum and Bacilllus licheniformis, which showed 28.1, 21.5 and 13.3% sequence identity, respectively, and were characterized as Zn2+-dependent d-serine dehydratases (data not shown). Dsd1p contains 1 mol of Zn2+ per protein monomer (6). In the recently solved crystal structure of chDsd, Zn2+ was found to be located in the active site and is held by two residues, a His and a Cys residue (His347 and Cys349), as well as by water molecules (8, Fig. 1). In Dsd1p, the Zn2+ is dispensable for substrate binding, but indispensable for both α-hydrogen abstraction and hydroxyl group elimination from d-serine (9).

We investigated the reaction mechanism of the unique Zn2+- and PLP-dependent d-serine dehydratase and suggest the following reaction mechanism for Dsd1p (Scheme I). PLP initially forms a Schiff base with Lys57 (internal aldimine, intermediate I). The reaction begins with the formation of d-serine-PLP external aldimine (intermediate II). Then, Lys57 abstracts an α-proton from the external aldimine, and the hydroxyl group is eliminated to yield an α-aminoacrylate intermediate (intermediate IV). Two mechanisms, E1cB and E2, can be supposed for the hydroxyl group elimination. In the E1cB mechanism, elimination occurs subsequent to the removal of the α-proton, resulting in the formation of a carbanionic intermediate(s) (intermediate III). In the E2 mechanism, α-proton abstraction and hydroxyl group elimination occur in concert without the formation of the carbanionic intermediates. The Dsd1p reaction is completed upon transaldimination by Lys57, releasing α-aminoacrylate, which is subsequently non-enzymatically hydrolyzed to pyruvate and ammonia.

Crystallography analysis has revealed the unique structural features of chDsd (8). chDsd has a conserved Tyr residue (Y174) at the position interacting with the pyridine nitrogen (N1) of PLP (the corresponding residue of Dsd1p is Y203, Fig. 1), which is unique among PLP enzymes. Unlike Dsd1p, various PLP-dependent enzymes such as aminotransferase and decarboxylase use an acidic residue (Asp or Glu) to interact with and protonate the N1 nitrogen of PLP. The protonated N1, acting as an electron sink, stabilizes the carbanionic intermediates, which are indispensable to the PLP enzymes that catalyze transamination, decarboxylation, aldol and Claisen condensations and lyase reactions with a substrate having a poor leaving group (10, 11). The presence of the Tyr residue suggests that protonation of the N1 nitrogen is not a prerequisite for the catalytic activity of Dsd1p.

In this study, we investigated the mechanistic significance of Y203 as well as the protonated state of the pyridine nitrogen of Dsd1p. The results indicate that the Tyr residue does not participate in the protonation of the N1 nitrogen, and Dsd1p uses PLP in an N1 unprotonated state. The Dsd1p reaction proceeds through the E1cB mechanism without forming stabilized carbanionic intermediates. These features promote hydroxyl group elimination and prevent Cα reprotonation before hydroxyl group protonation.

Materials and Methods
Materials
d-Serine, reduced form of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NADH), and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) from pig heart were from Wako (Osaka, Japan). Deuterium oxide was from Sigma-Aldrich (St Louis, MO, USA). PLP was from Tokyo Kasei (Tokyo, Japan). Oligonucleotides were from Operon (Tokyo, Japan).

Enzymes
Wild-type of d-serine dehydratase from S. cerevisiae (Dsd1p, C-terminal His-tag) was prepared as previously described (9). Single mutation was introduced into Tyr203 (Y203) using a set of the complementary primers containing a desired mutation. Primers sequences were as follows (where base changes are underlined): 5′-catatgggttttttgctcatgccggac-3′ (for Y203F), 5′-catatgggtttgctgctcatgccggac-3′ (Y203A), 5′- catatgggtttgatgctcatgccgga-3′ (Y203D), 5′-catatgggtttgaagctcatgccggac-3′ (Y203E), 5′-catatgggtttcgtgctcatgccggac-3′ (Y203R) 5′-catatgggttttctgctcatgccggac-3′ (Y203S). The mutation was confirmed by DNA sequencing. The resulting plasmid expressing mutated Dsd1p was introduced into E. coli KRX (Promega, Madison, WI, USA). Cell culturing, protein extraction, enzyme purification with Ni2+ affinity and anion exchange column chromatographies were conducted as previously reported (6, 9).

Enzyme assay
Kinetics of the mutant Dsd1ps were determined using the LDH-coupling method as described previously (5, 6). The reaction were performed in a buffer containing 50 mM HEPES−NaOH (pH 8.0), 50 µM PLP, 0.05−100 mM d-serine, 0.3 mM NADH, 10 U LDH and purified Dsd1p. The reaction mixture was incubated at 30°C in a cuvette of 1-cm light path and the rate of decrease in absorbance at 340 nm consequent upon NADH oxidation was determined using Shimadzu UV-2450 spectrophotometer.

Spectroscopic analysis
UV−visible spectrum was obtained in a 50 mM HEPES−NaOH (pH 8.0) at 25°C in a cuvette of 1-cm light path using Shimadzu UV-2450 spectrophotometer. d-Serine concentrations were 20 mM (for wild-type, Y203F and Y203A) or 100 mM (for other mutants).

1H NMR analysis
Changes in the 1H NMR spectra of d-serine were recorded at 27°C in 5-mm NMR tubes using a Bruker AMX-600 spectrometer operated at 600 MHz as described previously (9). The buffer and chemicals used were dissolved in 2H2O. The solvent for the enzyme was replaced with 10 mM potassium phosphate buffer (KPB) (p2H 8.0) by repeated concentration and dilution with an Amicon Ultra-15 (Millipore, Bedford, MA, USA). The reaction mixture was 10 mM KPB (p2H 8.0), 10 mM d-[α-1H]serine, 50 µM PLP and 0.5 mM 3-trimethylsilyl-1-propanesulfonate (DSS) as an internal standard. Y203F and Y203D were added to the reaction mixture at a final concentration of 0.038 and 0.14 mg/ml, respectively. The 1H signals of DSS appeared at −0.2, 0.45, 1.57 and 2.73 ppm. Among them, the signal appeared at −0.2 ppm. was used as an internal standard.

Results
The effect of mutating Tyr203 on the catalytic activity of Dsd1p
Dsd1p uses its highly conserved Tyr residue (Y203) to interact with the pyridine nitrogen of PLP (Fig. 1). To investigate the role of Y203 in catalysis, we first constructed the Y203F mutant enzyme. The Y203F mutant enzyme was obtained from a soluble fraction in E. coli cells and was purified using the same procedure as that for the wild-type enzyme (9). As shown in Table I, the Y203F mutant is a functionally conserved mutant. The kcat and Km values of d-serine dehydration catalyzed by Y203F were 4.3 s−1 and 0.7 mM, respectively. As judged by the kcat value, Y203F retains ∼25% of the wild-type enzyme activity. Mutants Y203A, Y203R and Y203S showed decreased d-serine dehydrase activity, but all of these retained substantial levels of the activity. The kcat values of Y203A, Y203R and Y203S were 14, 2.9 and 14% of the wild-type enzyme, respectively (Table I). These observations demonstrate that, unlike other PLP-dependent enzymes such as aminotransferases and decarboxylases, a protonated pyridine nitrogen is not required for the catalytic activity of Dsd1p.

In contrast, the catalytic activities of Y203D and Y203E were severely compromised. The kcat and Km values of Y203D were 0.097 s−1 and 8.5 mM, and those of Y203E were 0.083 s−1 and 5.6 mM, respectively (Table I). In both enzymes, the kcat values were ∼0.5% of that of the wild-type enzyme and the catalytic efficiency (kcat/Km) of the mutants decreased by 105-fold. These observations suggest that the protonated pyridine nitrogen is disadvantageous for the catalysis.

The enzyme activities of all mutant enzymes examined were Zn2+-dependent. All the enzymes lost their activities by EDTA treatment and fully recovered after the addition of Zn2+ (data not shown).

UV–visible spectra of Tyr203 mutants
The effects of Y203 mutation on the electronic state of PLP were examined by UV–visible spectrum analysis. The Y203F mutant enzyme showed absorption maxima at 278 and 408 nm (Fig. 2A and B). The latter peak has been ascribed to a ketoenamine tautomer of internal aldimine. When d-serine was added to the mutant enzyme, the absorbance at 330 nm attributed to the formed pyruvate increased without changing the λmax at around 408 nm. These spectral properties were almost identical to that of the wild-type enzyme (9). The lack of absorption peaks at around 470 and 500 nm suggests little or no accumulation of α-aminoacrylate or quinonoid intermediates, respectively (Fig. 2B). UV–visible spectrum analyses were also performed using Y203A, Y203R and Y203S. All of the mutants exhibited peaks at 278 nm and at around 410 nm, which is essentially the same as that for the wild-type enzyme. The addition of d-serine to the mutant enzymes induced a spectral change similar to that of the wild-type enzyme; the absorbance at 330 nm was increased without changing the absorbance at around 410 nm. No new peaks appeared at around 470 and 500 nm (data not shown).
As shown in Fig. 2A, C and D, the spectroscopic properties were altered when Y203 was changed to a negatively charged Asp or Glu. UV–vis spectrum of Y203D exhibited peaks at 278 and 390 nm, and the absorption maximum of the latter peak (λmax = 390 nm) was slightly different from that of the wild-type enzyme (λmax = 410 nm). Free PLP has an absorption maximum of around 390 nm. On the other hand, Hayashi et al. reported that the ketoenamine tautomer of the l-dopa-PLP Schiff base in the rat liver aromatic l-amino acid decarboxylase exhibits a peak at around 380 nm, which may be attributed to changes in environment of the active site such as the formation of new hydrogen bonds on either PLP or the substrate, or the non-planar structure of the external aldimine with its imine group perpendicular to the ring (12). The addition of NaCNBH3, a Schiff base reducing reagent, to Y203D resulted in a decrease in absorbance at 390 nm, with a concomitant increase at around 340 nm (data not shown). This suggests that although the Schiff base typically exhibits an absorption peak within the range of 400–440 nm, the peak at 390 nm represents an internal Schiff base rather than a free PLP. Upon addition of d-serine, the 390-nm peak immediately showed a red-shift, reflecting an external Schiff base formation (Fig. 2C, line of 2 min). The incubation of Y203D with d-serine yielded a peak at around 330 nm (Fig. 2C). The increase in the absorbance at 330 nm was derived from pyruvate formation, but not from pyridoxamine 5′-phosphate (PMP). The lack of PMP formation was confirmed by fluorescent spectral analysis excited at 330 nm and the direct determination of PMP by HPLC (data not shown). No absorption was observed at ∼500 nm with d-serine, indicating little accumulation of a quinonoid intermediate during the catalysis. Spectral properties similar to those of Y203D were obtained with Y203E under the same conditions. Y203E exhibited absorption maxima at 278 and 397 nm (Fig. 2D), and the latter peak was decreased by the addition of NaCNBH3. The addition of D-serine caused a red-shift of the λmax and pyruvate formation, although accumulation of a quinonoid intermediate was not observed during UV–visible spectral analyses (Fig. 2D).

N1 protonation promotes Cα reprotonation
To obtain more information on the effect of Y203 mutations on acidic residues, the rate of α-proton abstraction (v(α-proton abstraction)), leaving group elimination (v(OH elimination)) and α-proton/deuterium exchange (reprotonation at Cα, v(Cα reprotonation)) catalyzed by Y203D were separately determined using the 1H NMR technique as previously described (9). d-Serine (d-[α-1H]serine) was incubated with Y203D in D2O and the time-dependent disappearances of the α-proton and β-proton signals of d-serine were examined (Fig. 3A and B). The rates of decrease in the α-proton and β-proton signals were fitted to a single exponential function: formula for the decay of α-proton signals, and formula for the β-proton signals. The time-dependent decrease in the enzymatic activity was probably due to the high Km value of the mutant enzyme (8.5 mM, Table I) and/or the time-dependent inactivation of the mutant enzyme caused by the long-term incubation. The initial v(α-proton abstraction), v(OH elimination) and v(Cα reprotonation) were determined to be 0.104, 0.050 and 0.053 s−1, respectively, taking into consideration the amount of the enzyme present in the assay (Table II). Interestingly, the v(Cα reprotonation) was 51% of v(α-proton abstraction). The v(α-proton abstraction), v(OH elimination) and v(Cα reprotonation) catalyzed by the wild-type enzyme were 9.8, 8.5 and 1.2 s−1, respectively, and the v(Cα reprotonation) was 12% of v(α-proton abstraction) (9). The ratio of the rate of Cα reprotonation to that of the hydroxyl group elimination in the Y203D reaction was at least 4-fold higher than the ratio of the wild-type enzyme reaction. This indicate that the free energy barrier for the α-proton reprotonation was reduced to almost the same level as that for the following step such as protonation or elimination of the hydroxyl group.

Reaction specificity of Y203D
The protonated N1 of PLP is commonly used in aminotransferases and decarboxylases. Furthermore, in alanine racemase, it is known that the mutation of an Arg residue (R219) interacting with the N1 of PLP to Glu opened the possibility for the occurrence of a side reaction such as transamination (13, 14). We then examined the presence of side reactions such as transamination and decarboxylation with Y203D and Y203E. No PMP formation (occurrence of half reaction of transamination) was detected with d-serine, d-threonine or d-alanine, which was confirmed by the UV–vis spectra analysis, fluorescence spectra analysis excited at 330 nm, and the direct determination of PMP by HPLC (data not shown). In addition, these three amino acids were incubated with the mutant enzymes in the presence or absence of pyruvate, hydroxypyruvate and/or α-ketoglutarate, and then the occurrence of transamination, decarboxylation and/or Cα–Cβ bond cleavage were examined. No new amino acids and/or amines were generated under the conditions examined. These results indicate that mutants Y203D and Y203E retained high reaction specificities for dehydration.

Discussion
The electron sink ability of PLP is considered the principal driving force for the catalysis of PLP-dependent enzymes. Several PLP-dependent enzymes such as aminotransferases and decarboxylases use an acidic residue to interact with and protonate the pyridine nitrogen (N1) of PLP. N1 protonation enhances the electron sink ability of PLP and is favourable for the stabilization of a carbanionic intermediate formed during the reaction. Enzymes in which the N1 nitrogen is protonated, substitution of the residue to the non-acidic one imparts a critical effect on enzyme activity. For instance, the replacement of D222 to Ala and Arg in aspartate aminotransferase (AAT) leads to a ∼2 × 104-fold reduction in activity (15). The AAT reconstituted with 1-deaza-pyridoxal 5′-phosphate, a PLP analog lacking a pyridine nitrogen, showed a 109-fold lower activity compared with that of the wild-type enzyme (16). Mutation of the E274 in Trypanosoma brucei ornithine decarboxylase (ODC) resulted in a decrease in the kcat/Km by ∼600-fold; however, reconstitution of ODC with N-methyl-PLP instead of PLP restored the enzyme activity to the wild-type levels (17). On the other hand, some PLP enzymes use PLP in the N1-unprotonated state. O-acetylserine sulfhydrylase (OASS), which catalyzes an α, β-elimination reaction that eliminates acetate from O-acetylserine to form an aminoacrylate intermediate, equips a neutral serine residue (S272) to interact with the pyridine nitrogen of PLP. It has been reported that OASS catalyzes the reaction in an anti-E2 manner without forming a carbanionic intermediate, and the S272A mutation resulted only in a ∼4-fold decrease in the kcat/Km for the first half-reaction (18, 19). In alanine racemase of Bacillus stearothermophilus, an Arg residue (R219) directly donates a hydrogen bond to the pyridine nitrogen of PLP, which prevents the protonation of N1 of PLP (20). As previously described, Dsd1p equips a Tyr residue whose pKa in solution is ∼10 to interact with the pyridine nitrogen of PLP. The Tyr residue is highly conserved in the Dsd1p family of enzymes, suggesting that it plays a significant role in the catalysis.

As shown in Table I, the mutant enzymes in which Y203 was replaced by a non-polar or a basic residue retained substantial activity (>3% in kcat). Among these, Y203F showed the least impact on catalytic activity. Y203R also retained ∼3% of the wild-type enzyme activity, as indicated by its kcat value. In contrast, the values of Y203D and Y203E decreased by ∼200-fold (∼0.5% in kcat, Table I). These findings suggest that the protonated pyridine nitrogen is not required for the catalytic activity of Dsd1p. Dsd1p probably uses PLP in an N1-unprotonated state for optimal activity, and the protonation of N1 is rather disadvantageous for the catalytic activity of the enzyme. It is also possible that Y203 plays a role in maintaining the N1 in an unprotonated state, as shown by the high pKa value of its phenolic side-chain.

The kcat/Km value of Y203F for d-serine dehydration was ∼15-fold lower than that of the wild-type enzyme, whereas that of Y203D and Y203E was ∼105-fold lower (Table I). These findings suggest that d-serine dehydration may proceed through an E2 mechanism, as reported in OASS (18, 19). In the E2 mechanism, α-proton abstraction and leaving group elimination occurs via a concerted mechanism and no carbanionic intermediate is formed during the reaction. However, in the E2 mechanism, the Cα–H and the hydroxyl group of d-serine should be situated antiperiplanar. The structural model of the chDSD-d-serine complex suggests that both of the Cα–H and the hydroxyl group of d-serine is located within a distance of 3 Å from Lys45 at the reface of PLP, which is not antiperiplanar in stereochemistry (8). In addition, 1H NMR analyses demonstrated that the v(α-proton abstraction), the v(OH elimination) and the v(Cα reprotonation) of the wild-type enzyme was 9.8, 8.5 and 1.2 s−1, respectively, and those catalyzed by Y203F were 4.7, 3.0 and 1.7 s−1, respectively (Table II). The presence of the Cα reprotonation provides direct evidence that Dsd1p yields a carbanionic intermediate before eliminating the hydroxyl group in an E1cB mechanism. Although the reaction proceeds through the E1cB mechanism, α-proton abstraction and hydroxyl group elimination occur almost coincidentally. A carbanionic intermediate probably exists only for a short time and Cα-reprotonation hardly occurs in the wild-type and Y203F mutant enzymes.

The 1H NMR analysis demonstrated that the frequency of Cα reprotonation (v(Cα reprotonation)/v(α-proton abstraction)) was 0.12 in the wild-type enzyme, whereas that of Y203D was 0.51 (Table II). This indicates that the free energy barrier for α-proton reprotonation was reduced to almost the same level as that for the following steps, as well as the transition state between intermediate II (Scheme I) and III is closer to intermediate III than the transition state between intermediate III and IV in Y203D reaction. It is known that the reduction in the Cα pKa value was achieved by the protonation of the pyridine nitrogen of the cofactor. Major and Gao (21) performed combined quantum mechanical/molecular mechanical simulations to investigate the origin of the carbon acidity enhancement in the alanine racemase reaction. They reported that the formation of the N1-protonated form of Ala-PLP aldimine can reduce the pKa of Cα by 22 units, whereas the N1-unprotonated form of Ala-PLP results in a reduction by 13 units, indicating that the protonation of N1 lowers the Cα carbon acidity by ∼8 units (21). In addition, Casasnovas et al. (22) recently estimated that protonation of the pyridine nitrogen in Gly-PLP in the ketoenamine form reduces the pKa of Cα by 5.6 units compared with that of the N1-unprotonated form. Therefore, it is most probably that the protonation of N1 enhances Cα carbon acidity, stabilizes the carbanion intermediate, and affects the levels of free energy barrier for the α-proton reprotonation and the following steps.

This study has shown that Dsd1p uses PLP in an N1-unprotonated state. Another mechanism for enhancing the Cα carbon acidity may exist in the Dsd1p reaction. As described earlier, in alanine racemase, R219 interacts with the N1 of PLP and maintains its unprotonated state. A second Arg residue (R136) interacts with the phenolic oxygen (O3′ of PLP) and the carboxyl group of the Ala-PLP external aldimine. Major and Gao (21) performed a computational study and revealed that both of the Arg residues (R219 and R136) equally contribute to the stabilization of the transition state in the alanine racemase reaction. Interestingly, a similar situation involving the presence of an Arg residue (R143) proximal to the phenol oxygen O3′ and the carboxyl group of external aldimine has been observed in chDsd (8). R143 is highly conserved among the Dsd1p protein family, and R171 is the corresponding residue of Dsd1p (Fig. 1). These findings suggest that in Dsd1p, the second Arg residue (R171) probably plays an important role in delocalizing the negative charge. Casasnovas et al. (22) reported that the protonation state of phenol oxygen O3′ determines the relative acidity of Cα and C4′, and that the presence of R136 might be responsible for the high specificity of racemization of the enzyme by preventing C4′ protonation. Therefore, the presence of the R171 in Dsd1p may be required to prevent transamination as a side reaction, in addition to delocalization of the negative charge of the intermediate. To examine these speculations, further investigations including mutational analysis of R171 would be required.

In conclusion, we have revealed that Y203 is not involved in the protonation of pyridine nitrogen of PLP, and Dsd1p uses PLP in an N1 unprotonated state. The N1-unprotonated state of PLP yields a carbanionic intermediate with a short lifetime, which most likely aids in the elimination of the hydroxyl group by preventing Cα reprotonation before the protonation of the leaving group.

Dcs2, a novel stress-induced modulator of m7GpppX pyrophosphatase activity that locates to P bodies

Abstract
The eukaryotic “scavenger” type decapping enzyme, an m7GpppX pyrophosphatase, is active in cellular mRNA metabolism and thereby influences posttranscriptional gene expression. The yeast version of this enzyme, Dcs1, catalyses cleavage of 5′end m7G-oligoribonucleotide fragments generated by 3′→5′ exonucleolytic decay, and cleavage of m7GDP generated by Dcp1/Dcp2-mediated decapping in the 5′→3′ decay pathway. We show that Dcs1 is active as a homodimer with low KM values for cleavage of m7GpppG (0.14 μM) and m7GDP (0.26 μM). Previous work showed that the paralogous DCS2 gene is transcriptionally induced via the amp-PKA pathway as yeast enters diauxie. The resulting Dcs2 protein forms a heterodimer together with Dcs1, both modulating Dcs1 substrate specificity and suppressing its kcat. Since Dcs2 is recruited into cytoplasmic P bodies, its inhibitory function may be focused in these centres of mRNA storage/turnover. Dcs2 is therefore a novel type of stress-induced regulatory protein that modulates m7GpppX pyrophosphatase activity. Moreover, inhibition of Dcs1 activity by Dcs2, like depletion of Dcs1, reduces chronological life span, possibly by modulating m7G misincorporation into nucleic acids. This could potentially link control of mRNA metabolism with senescence.

Introduction
Enzyme-catalysed degradation processes constitute key steps in the turnover of the diverse species of mRNA found in eukaryotic cells, and thus contribute significantly to the posttranscriptional control of gene expression.1,2 The degradation of the body of eukaryotic mRNA is performed largely by exonucleases, whereby access of these enzymes requires removal of either the 3′poly(A) tail, the 5′cap, or of both.3., 4., 5. Decapping is an important rate-controlling step, since it exposes the 5′end of mRNAs to attack by 5′→3′ exonucleases of the Xrn1 type.6,7 Work in the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae has identified two proteins, Dcp1 and Dcp2, as involved in m7GDP-generating decapping, and homologues of these proteins exist in higher eukaryotes.7., 8., 9. Residues critical for the m7GDP-generating cleavage activity are present in the Nudix motif of Dcp2, and this protein is selective for mRNA substrates longer than eight nucleotides.10 There has been uncertainty whether Dcp1 manifests (comparatively low) catalytic activity within the Dcp1:Dcp2 complex, acts only as an enhancer of Dcp2 activity, or performs both roles,8,10,11 but there is now no doubt that Dcp2 is the major m7GDP-generating decapping enzyme.
An m7GMP-generating decapping activity that was originally detected in mammalian cell extracts12,13 has more recently been identified as DcpS, a “scavenger” decapping enzyme with a histidine triad (HIT) pyrophosphatase motif.3 Related enzymes have been identified in S.cerevisiae (Dcs1)14,15 and in Schizosaccharomyces pombe (Nhm1).16 DcpS was shown to act as a scavenging pyrophosphatase that helps mop up short, capped mRNA fragments left over from 3′→5′ exonucleolytic decay.3 However, since the human and S.cerevisiae proteins also cleave m7GDP,17 which is generated by Dcp1/Dcp2 cleavage, Dcs-type enzymes are now thought to act in both the 3′→5′ and 5′→3′ pathways. Very recently, it has been shown that Dcs1 activity is required for maintenance of the normal rate of 5′→3′ exoribonucleolytic decay.18
The 5′cap also plays important roles in other processes. This modification is essential for the efficient translation of cellular mRNAs.19 In the nucleus, apart from protecting the 5′end from exonucleolytic degradation, it promotes polyadenylation and export from the nucleus20,21 as well as certain splicing events.22 The nuclear functions of the cap are generally (but not necessarily exclusively) dependent upon binding to the nuclear cap-binding complex (CBC).23 Experimental work performed in vitro has shown that the presence of cap analogues such as m7GpppG or m7GTP can inhibit cap-dependent processes. This type of study has revealed that these analogues are strongly inhibitory in the 10–100 μM range. The intracellular concentrations of m7G-(oligo)ribonucleotides (from m7GDP to m7GpppXn) are therefore of significance to several processes. This, in turn, highlights a further dimension to the DcpS/Dcs1 type activity, since these enzymes play a central role in m7G-(oligo)ribonucleotide turnover. Moreover, a still unresolved issue is whether dinucleoside polyphosphates24 or m7G-(oligo)ribonucleotides15,18 have specific roles in cellular signalling. Cleavage of at least some (m7G-containing) members of this group of nucleotide species by the DcpS/Dcs1 type of enzyme therefore suggests a possible link to signalling pathways, but this possibility has yet to be investigated.
Both dcs-1 in Caenorhabditis elegans and DCS1 in S.cerevisiae are subject to transcriptional induction in response to stress.15,25,26 However, in S.cerevisiae, the homologous DCS2 gene undergoes a far greater positive step-change in expression under diauxic conditions than DCS1.15 Dcs2 manifests 65% identity and 90% similarity to Dcs1, yet the function of the Dcs2 protein, which has no detectable pyrophosphatase activity,14 has remained a mystery. The absence of a dcs2Δ phenotype during log-phase growth on glucose has been explained on the basis that this gene is only expressed after nutrient stress induction,15 and thus our recent attention has focused on the function of DCS2 in the induced state.
Here, we have made a number of unexpected discoveries concerning the functional role of Dcs2. This protein appears to be a novel type of cap-cleavage modulator that is used by the cell to impose suppression of Dcs1 activity in response to nutrient stress.

Results
Stress-dependent Dcs1:Dcs2 heterodimer formation
We showed previously that DCS2 expression is barely detectable during logarithmic growth on glucose.15 As cellular metabolism becomes glucose-limited, DCS2 expression is switched on at the transcriptional level. We have now investigated the fate of the Dcs2 protein thereby generated in yeast cells using two complementary approaches (Figure 1). First, pull-down experiments using a FLAG-tagged version of Dcs2 revealed the accumulation of Dcs1:Dcs2 heterodimer after stress-induced synthesis of Dcs2 as cells run short of glucose (Figure 1(a)). This confirmed formation of the heterodimer observed previously15 and demonstrated that dimerization is not an artefactual event caused by the addition of the TAP tag. Second, the shift of Dcs1 from homodimer into Dcs1:Dcs2 heterodimer as cells progress through diauxie is clearly demonstrated by Western blot analysis of the fractionation profile obtained by means of gel filtration of extracts derived from a strain synthesising TAP-tagged Dcs2 (PTC197, see Table 1 for strains; Figure 1(b)). In a control experiment, we used a (wild-type) strain (PTC5; BY4741) that synthesizes Dcs2 but not the Dcs2-TAP fusion, in which case no Dcs1 was pulled into the higher molecular mass region occupied by the Dcs2-TAP:Dcs1 heterodimer, but rather ran in the lower molecular mass region (approximately 80 kDa) expected of the untagged heterodimer (Figure 1(b)). As reported previously,15 Dcs1 runs as a double band in these experiments because some of the protein is phosphorylated. Here, we observed that the heterodimer complex contains somewhat more of the unphosphorylated form than of the phosphorylated form (Figure 1(b)). However, in additional experiments (data not shown) we found no evidence that phosphorylation exerts a significant effect on Dcs1 activity or protein distribution within the cell, and therefore did not pursue this line of investigation further.

Dcs2 inhibits Dcs1 function
Having observed formation of the Dcs1:Dcs2 heterodimer in diauxic yeast, we considered whether this species has properties distinct from those of the Dcs1 homodimer. In order to answer this question, we compared the catalytic behaviour of the heterodimeric and homodimeric isoforms. We first used Dcs1 purified from S.cerevisiae (Materials and Methods) in a cap cleavage assay. This was performed with the substrates m7GpppG (Figure 2(a); Table 2) and m7GDP (Table 2). For the derivation of Michaelis-Menten parameters, the resulting initial rate data for m7GpppG were used to construct Lineweaver-Burk and Eadie-Hofstee plots (Figure 2(b)). We estimated that the Dcs1 homodimer has a KM of 0.14 μM for m7GpppG and a KM of 0.26 μM for m7GDP (Table 2). The low KM values of Dcs1 mean that this enzyme is capable of maintaining high specific cleavage activity down to sub-micromolar intracellular concentrations of m7GDP and m7G-capped mRNA fragments. It therefore seems to be appropriately adapted to clear the various m7G-(oligo)ribonucleotide species generated by the mRNA decay pathways from the cell. In further experiments (data not shown), we found that the Dcs2 homodimer15 showed no measurable cleavage activity against m7GpppG, m7GDP or a capped 20mer, confirming the lack of cleavage of m7GpppG observed previously.14 Indeed, unlike Dcs1, Dcs2 showed far lower affinity for m7GTP-Sepharose 4B (Figure 1(c)); while 80% of the bound Dcs1 could be specifically eluted by m7GpppG (lane 4), ≥ 95% of the Dcs2 was found in the flow-through fraction (lane 2).

We next studied the properties of the Dcs1:Dcs2 heterodimer (Figure 3). The heterodimer can be purified from strains in which TAP-tagged versions of the Dcs1 (PTC196, DCS1::TAP) and Dcs2 (PTC197, DCS2::TAP) proteins are synthesised15 (Figure 3(a) and Materials and Methods). Both the phosphorylated and non-phosphorylated forms of Dcs1 were pulled down in these experiments, and thus the total amount of Dcs1 was given by the sum of the two populations. Control experiments using appropriate dcs1Δ and dcs2Δ strains confirmed the necessity for expression of both genes for formation of the heterodimer bands (Figure 3(a)). Of particular importance was the observation that neither untagged Dcs1 nor untagged Dcs2 could be pulled down from extracts derived from the (wild-type) strain PTC5 (BY4741; Figure 3(a)). This means, in turn, that preparations of Dcs1:Dcs2-CBD pulled down from strain PTC197 (DCS2::TAP) extracts will not be contaminated by Dcs1:Dcs1 homodimer. Moreover, examination of the complete lanes on a silver-stained gel loaded with the respective dimer preparations reveals that these preparations are highly pure (Supplementary Figure 2).
We first compared the rates of m7GpppG hydrolysis catalysed by a series of dilutions of Dcs1:Dcs2-CBD heterodimer (prepared from PTC197 (DCS2::TAP)) with the rates obtained using equivalent Dcs1 homodimer dilutions (Figure 3(b)). We were able to employ equivalent amounts of heterodimer and homodimer in these experiments by carefully standardizing concentrations (see Supplementary Figure 5). This comparison revealed that the rate of hydrolysis is linearly related to enzyme concentration, and that the heterodimer shows a marked reduction (relative to Dcs1 homodimer) in the rates of cleavage of m7GpppG and m7GDP. The reduction in the rate of cleavage of a capped 20mer was at least as pronounced (Figure 3(c)), but the ratio was not quantified accurately in this work because the absolute rates observed with this longer substrate are far lower. There were probably some shorter m7G32ppp-capped species in the 20mer preparation (see smear in Figure 3(c)), but these data are presented only as an approximate indicator of the relative competence to cleave longer substrates. Initial rate analyses revealed that the heterodimer manifests reduced kcat values (eightfold and 3.4-fold, respectively) and increased KM values (7.2-fold and 2.9-fold, respectively) for m7GpppG and m7GDP (Figure 3(f); Table 2). As might be expected for inhibition involving complex formation with Dcs1 but not binding to the active site, this kinetic behaviour suggests that Dcs2 does not act via a simple competitive mechanism with respect to substrate–Dcs1 interactions.
In order to gain more insight into the influence of Dcs2 in vivo, we examined cap cleavage rates observed using total extracts from different log-phase cultures of S.cerevisiae (Figure 3(d) and (e)). During log phase growth there is normally almost no Dcs2 present in the cells to inhibit Dcs1 activity.15 Therefore, we reasoned that an informative indication of the ability of Dcs2 to inhibit Dcs1 activity in vivo would be to check the effects of expressing DCS2 during log phase growth. The results of this experiment were consistent with the observation of inhibition of Dcs1 by Dcs2 in purified dimer preparations derived from early stationary phase cells of PTC197 (DCS2::TAP; Figure 3(b)), in that the appearance of Dcs2 in the early log phase cells of (wild-type) PTC5 (BY4741; Figure 3(e)) was accompanied by attenuation of Dcs1 activity in total cell extracts (Figure 3(d)). Taken together, these data confirm the notion that Dcs2 is a specific inhibitor of Dcs1 that can function in both rapidly growing and quiescent cells.
In further experiments, we found that addition of Dcs2 homodimer purified from yeast to the log phase extract does not suppress Dcs1 activity (Supplementary Figure 6; the same negative result was obtained using recombinant Dcs1 and Dcs2 derived from E.coli (data not shown)). These results are likely to be due to a low exchange rate for monomers that have already been incorporated into a dimer complex. We interpret this to mean that Dcs2 is only effectively incorporated into the heterodimer via binding of (de novo synthesized) monomers.
Dcs2 localizes to cytoplasmic foci
Having established that Dcs2 is a nutrient stress-dependent regulator of Dcs1, we wanted to understand the spatial context in which the Dcs proteins operate. In a previous study,15 we used immunofluorescence microscopy to reveal the largely cytoplasmic distributions of epitope-tagged Dcs proteins in formaldehyde-fixed cells. Here, we chose a less disruptive method to study the dynamics of these distributions as cells progress through diauxie. This involved the construction of chromosomal GFP-DCS fusions that are expressed from the natural promoters at endogenous levels (compare, for example, Sheff and Parker27 with Brengues et al.28). In the early phase of induction of Dcs2 synthesis, the comparatively small amount of Dcs2 is predominantly cytoplasmic and relatively diffuse, although there may be some accumulation in what appears to be the perinuclear space (Figure 4(a)). Interestingly, this correlates with the appearance of some Dcs1 close to the nuclear region in log phase cells (Figure 4(a)). However, as the culture approaches late-log-phase, most of the Dcs2 protein becomes recruited to foci, and the latter progressively increase in size as glucose starvation becomes more extreme (Figure 4(b)). In contrast, Dcs1 remains relatively evenly distributed in the cytoplasm, including the P bodies, as cells progress into stationary phase (data not shown). We observed a dramatic increase in the frequency of cells with Dcs2-containing foci as cells progressed into diauxie (Figure 4(c)). Although we did not attempt to image through all sections of all cells and therefore cannot provide absolute values for the percentage of cells manifesting Dcs2-containing foci, it is likely that the vast majority of diauxic cells contain these bodies.
This raised the question whether the foci identified using the GFP-Dcs fusions are identical to the P-bodies described previously in yeast and mammalian cells.27,29 We therefore tested for co-localization with the decapping activator protein Lsm1 (Figure 5), which has been shown previously to locate to P bodies.27 Moreover, in additional experiments (Supplementary Figure 3), we also found that Lsm1 colocalizes with the major decapping protein Dcp2 in the same foci, thus confirming the identification of these foci as P bodies in our strains. Taken together, these results allow us to conclude that a significant proportion of the Dcs2 protein is recruited to the P bodies in response to diauxie. The progressive enlargement of these bodies during stationary phase has also been observed in an earlier study of the localization of major decay pathway components.30 We also conclude that, while much of the heterodimer is expected to form within the P bodies, it will not be exclusively formed in these bodies, since a (lower) intensity of GFP-Dcs2 fluorescence is distributed throughout the cytoplasm.
Dcs1 and Dcs2 have opposing effects on chronological life span
Dcs1 activity is known to generate decapped oligoribonucleotides, m7GMP and phosphate through hydrolysis of its range of substrates.18 We performed some preliminary experiments to assess whether changes in the abundance of these products might result in variations in the levels of m7G misincorporated into RNA during transcription. Adapting a procedure used previously to study methylation of tRNA guanosine bases,31 we measured the concentration of m7G incorporated into total RNA in strains lacking tRNA methylation (see trm8Δ strains PTC216–219, Table 1). We observed an increase of between 10 and 100 nM in the m7G concentration in RNA extracts from dcs1Δ cells (data not shown). The levels of m7G detected were too close to the resolution limit of the analytical technique to allow accurate quantification, but did indicate that Dcs1 activity affects m7G content in cellular RNA. Since there is enhanced Dcs1 activity in the dcs2Δ background (Supplementary Figure 6), this also suggests that Dcs2 may influence m7G misincorporation into RNA. Moreover, since GDP is converted to dGDP in S. cerevisiae,32,33 m7GDP can also be converted to m7dGDP and then to m7dGTP, thus introducing m7G into the pool of nucleotides used for DNA synthesis. While m7dG is not expected to affect DNA duplex structure or coding, increased levels in DNA may lead to increased levels of toxic repair intermediates generated by the base excision repair (BER) system (see, for example, Rinne et al.34).
One expected effect of misincorporation of m7G into nucleic acids is an accumulation of mutational changes over time. In non-dividing (postmitotic) cells, malfunctioning cellular components generated by erroneous gene expression (partly prior to exhaustion of glucose) cannot be diluted out by cell growth and division, and thus the effects of such errors may be magnified once the cells reach the stationary phase. This consideration prompted us to examine the survival characteristics of our strains using a standard chronological life span assay.35 This measures the decline in viability of stationary phase cells as a function of time. Comparison of the survival statistics for wild-type, dcs1Δ, dcs2Δ and dcs1Δ dcs2Δ strains revealed that both Dcs1 and Dcs2 influence life span, but in contrasting ways (Figure 6(a)). Assessing the trends over the full course of the experiments, we see that deletion of DCS1 accelerated the chronological life span, whereas deletion of only DCS2 resulted in increased life span. These effects became most marked later in the time-course (particularly evident on day 16). Control experiments showed that these deviations from normal survival patterns are suppressed by complementation of the deficiency in Dcs1 activity (Figure 6(b)). Thus wild-type cells depend on Dcs1 activity to maintain a “normal” chronological life span, but Dcs2 is likely to prevent the cell from developing the full activity of the available Dcs1 enzyme. Once Dcs2 is removed, life span is enhanced, albeit only relatively late in the experimental time-course (Figure 6(a)). While the observed effects are relatively small, we are confident that they are significant because supplementary data attached to a very recent high throughput study of chronological life span in a different strain of yeast indicate very similar effects of the respective deletions.36 It is notable that the dcs1Δ dcs2Δ strain generally shows a shorter life span than the dcs2Δ strain, and that by 16 days the life spans of the dcs1Δ dcs2Δ and dcs1Δ strains are, within experimental error, identical. Overall, these results are consistent with the idea that Dcs2 influences longevity via its influence on Dcs1. This, in turn, suggests that the enhanced life span observed in the dcs2Δ strain could be related to the modulating effect that Dcs2 exerts on m7G(oligo)nucleotide metabolism.
Discussion
This study has revealed that Dcs2 represents a previously unknown subclass of the HIT-motif superfamily. It does not manifest pyrophosphatase activity itself, but rather binds to the m7GpppX cleaving enzyme Dcs1, inhibiting the latter's activity. The yeast cell restricts synthesis of Dcs2 to conditions of diauxic stress, under which Dcs2 is able to bind Dcs1 to form a heterodimer that has a kcat/KM value (depending on the substrate) that is up to 57 times smaller than that of the Dcs1 homodimer (Table 2). It is also informative to note the ratio of kcat/KM for m7GpppG to kcat/KM for m7GDP, since this ratio reflects the specificity of an enzyme for its respective substrates.37 The ratio is 13 for the Dcs1 homodimer and 2.1 for the Dcs1:Dcs2 heterodimer, showing that the latter has almost lost its preference for m7GpppG as a substrate. This suggests that while the Dcs1 homodimer cleaves the mRNA 5′cap structure considerably more efficiently than it cleaves m7GDP, Dcs1:Dcs2 will hydrolyse the two substrates at similar, albeit strongly attenuated, rates. This change in specificity might represent an adaptation to the changes in distribution and relative activities of the mRNA decay pathways (3′→5′ and 5′→3′) in the stationary phase cell.
A further unexpected feature of Dcs2 is that it is recruited to the P bodies of stationary phase cells. This recruitment will mean that the local levels of m7GDP and of m7G-oligoribonucleotides in what are suggested to be centres of mRNA turnover and/or storage will increase. Decreased Dcs1 activity is known to lead to inhibition of 5′→3′ exoribonucleolytic decay,18 and therefore our data suggest that Dcs2 activity will inhibit this pathway. The recruitment of Dcs2 to the location where much of the mRNA decay machinery is believed to be concentrated under conditions of nutrient stress suggests that this protein may contribute to attenuation of (primarily 5′→3′) decay activity within the P bodies. This would be consistent with the proposed function of P bodies as storage sites for mRNA in which the decay apparatus is at least partially active while the translation machinery is largely absent,28 although it has to be said that the function of P bodies remains a subject of considerable debate. At the same time, the inhibition of 5′→3′ degradative activity will shift the balance of contributions of the two major exonucleolytic pathways to the total decay rate. While Dcs2 will be present in excess over Dcs1 within the P bodies, the ratio will be lower elsewhere. The significance of this distribution in terms of the potential formation of concentration gradients of Dcs1 substrates in the cell is unknown. We should also note that we cannot rule out that Dcs2 function may not be restricted solely to its influence on Dcs1.
Diauxic conditions induce accelerated degradation of a subset of yeast mRNAs, while having no effect on, or even slowing, the decay of others.38 The mechanistic basis of this diversity of regulatory effects is not understood, but their complex nature leads us to believe that the effects of Dcs2-mediated modulation of decapping on mRNA decay under conditions of nutrient stress could be equally diverse, both in qualitative and quantitative terms. Certainly, our initial investigations of the effects of DCS2 deletion on the half-lives of a limited number of individual mRNAs (CDC33, PGK1, YAP1) have revealed only small effects (data not shown). On the other hand, the data reported here suggest that 5′→3′ decay outside of the P bodies will not be subject to such strong inhibition by Dcs2. As a result, the distribution of Dcs2 within the cell could potentially play a role in differential (and possibly spatially dependent) regulation of mRNA decay. From the above we conclude that full elucidation of the effects of Dcs2 action on mRNA stability will require transcriptome-wide array analysis of the effects of DCS2 mutation on the degradation of yeast transcripts under conditions of nutrient stress. Moreover, a more complete and precise characterisation of the function of P bodies would also help us understand why Dcs2 accumulates within them.
We have also seen that the chain of events that initiates with Dcs1 inhibition by Dcs2 ultimately leads to relatively small but reproducible changes in the chronological life span of yeast cells (see model in Figure 7). Mirroring this is the negative effect on chronological life span of deletion of the DCS1 gene, a phenomenon that may reflect the same underlying mechanism. The enhancement in chronological life span seen in dcs2Δ cells only becomes clearly evident late in the life span experiments (Figure 6(a)), reaching threefold by day 16. However, the reduction in chronological life span seen in dcs1Δ cells, which becomes clearly evident earlier in the life-span experiment and reaches maximally 12-fold (Figure 6(b)), is consistent with the operation of the proposed causal chain via suppression of Dcs1 activity. Moreover, the more pronounced (negative) effect of DCS1 deletion on life span is also quantitatively consistent with the dcs2Δ life span data, since the DCS1 deletion reduces Dcs1 activity more than does the inhibitory effect of the normal Dcs2 level in the cell. Interestingly, a very recent high-throughput study has identified a number of genes whose deletion causes changes in chronological life span of a similar magnitude38 (also see below).
The preliminary m7G misincorporation data mentioned here suggest an explanation for the effects of Dcs2 activity on chronological life span. The role of m7G is of particular interest because of the parallels in human cancer. An example is the guanosine methylation caused by tobacco carcinogens such as 4-(methylnitrosamino)-1-(3-pyridyl)-1-butanone, which is suspected to lead to lesions via the BER system.39 The accumulation of DNA lesions, internally methylated RNA and mutated proteins that is attributable to increased levels of m7G may explain the reduction in yeast cell longevity that is associated with Dcs2 activity. While this is not the focus of the current study, future research will need to address the mechanistic details of this potential link between the control of Dcs1 activity and changes in chronological life span that may be attributable to accumulated errors.
There seem to be relatively few genes in yeast whose expression reduces life-span.35,38,40 A small number of long-lived yeast deletion strains were recently discovered using a high-throughput screening procedure.38 These included strains lacking genes with a role in glutamine metabolism. Additionally, we conducted a bioinformatic search that identified RAS2, which is a homologue of the mammalian oncogene RAS.40 It encodes a small GTP-binding protein that apparently regulates a number of processes via its interaction with the adenylate cyclase Cyr1. These processes include sporulation, filamentous growth and the nitrogen starvation response. Thus, as in the case of DCS2, the life span of yeast can be extended by deletion of a gene that plays a role in this organism's response to nutrient stress. Indeed, it is possible that RAS2 may control life span via its influence on DCS2 expression, since cAMP synthesis influences STRE-dependent transcription. In terms of their respective influences on chronological life span, Dcs1 and Dcs2 lie on opposite faces of the same coin. Taken together with its stress-specific expression profile and mode of action, these attributes identify Dcs2 as a novel type of regulatory protein with wide-ranging effects.In terms of the selective advantage that might be conferred by possession of this type of gene, it seems that the yeast cell strikes a balance between the benefit of regulation of Dcs1 activity in diauxie when DCS2 is induced and the selective advantage of increased stationary-phase longevity that can be won when Dcs2 activity is suppressed.

Materials and Methods
Yeast strains and growth conditions, genetic manipulations
Yeast strains were as shown in Table 1. Northern blots confirmed the presence or absence of DCS1 and DCS2 mRNAs in the first series of deletion strains (PTC194, PTC143 (Y12429), PTC195; see Table 1 and Supplementary Figure 1). Cells were grown in liquid YPD (1% (w/v) yeast extract, 2% (w/v) peptone, 2% (w/v) glucose) or on plates containing YPD plus 2% (w/v) agar. For expression of DCS2 in log phase yeast cells, we used PCR to generate a fragment bearing the DCS2 gene plus 600 nucleotides on each side (including the natural DCS2 promoter) inserted into the yeast centromere vector pRS315 (LEU2 marker), as described.15
Separating homodimers and heterodimers by gel filtration
For gel filtration analysis, cell extracts were prepared from yeast strains PTC5 (BY4741; wild-type) and PTC197 (DCS2::TAP; Table 1). Two litres of cell culture at early log phase or 0.5 l of cell culture at late log phase were centrifuged at 4000 g for 10 min, cells were washed with buffer A (40 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.4), 120 mM NaCl, 0.1% NP-40, 5% (v/v) glycerol), resuspended in 15 ml of buffer A containing protease inhibitor cocktail (Sigma), and broken using 0.5 mm glass beads. The lysate was cleared by centrifugation at 8000 g for 20 min. The supernatant was separated from insoluble material and the lipid fraction by centrifugation at 29,000 g for 1 h and loaded onto a Superdex 200 HiLoad 16/60 column (Amersham) connected to a FPLC System (Pharmacia), and then equilibrated with 3 vol. of buffer A. The column was run at a flow rate of 0.5 ml/min at 4 °C. 1.5 ml protein fractions were collected and analysed by means of SDS/PAGE and Western blotting. The molecular mass was estimated by comparison with the elution of protein standards of alcohol dehydrogenase (150 kDa), bovine serum albumin (66 kDa) and chicken egg albumin (45 kDa) (standards obtained from Sigma).
Protein purification
Heterodimer and homodimer forms of Dcs1 and Dcs2 proteins were isolated from yeast to a high level of purity (we estimate ≥ 95%; see Supplementary Figure 2) using the tandem affinity purification (TAP) technique.41 Strains PTC196, PTC197, PTC214 and PTC215 were grown as 0.5 l cultures to the same point in late log phase. In order to avoid contamination by the heterodimer, Dcs1 homodimer was purified from strain PTC214 and Dcs2 homodimer was purified from strain PTC215. The Dcs1:Dcs2-CBD heterodimer was purified from strain PTC197. Cell extracts were prepared as described for gel filtration above. TAP purification was performed essentially as described,42 yielding proteins tagged by the short (44 residues long) calmodulin binding domain (CBD). Purified protein fractions were dialysed against buffer B (40 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.4), 120 mM NaCl, 5% glycerol) and stored at − 80 °C. Recombinant His-tagged Dcs2 protein that had been generated from the pET5A-DCS2 plasmid in Escherichia coli BL21(DE3) CodonPlus RIL cells was purified using a nickel affinity column (Novagen), followed by a Resource Q column (Amersham).15 Recombinant His-tagged Dcs1 protein was purified in a similar fashion, as described.15
Western blotting
Cell extracts were prepared, subjected to SDS-PAGE, transferred, and visualized as described.15 Dcs1, Dcs2-TAP and FLAG-Dcs2 proteins were detected using anti-Dcs1,15 PAP (peroxidase-anti-peroxidase, for protein A recognition) and anti-FLAG (both Sigma) antibodies, respectively.
Determination of chronological life span
Analysis of the chronological life span and statistical analysis of life-span differences were performed essentially as described.35 Cell cultures were grown aerobically at 30 °C in liquid YPDA medium (1% Difco yeast extract, 2% bactopeptone, 2% glucose, 20 mg/l adenine). Where necessary, selective pressure was imposed by growing the cells in minimal medium (YNB w/o amino acids, 2% glucose, 0.002% His, 0.002% Met, 0.003% Leu, 0.003% Lys, 0.002% Ura). Flask cultures were first inoculated from an overnight stationary YPDA culture to give an initial density of 5 × 105 cells/ml. These cultures were then grown to stationary phase in a rotary shaker set at 200 rpm. They were confirmed as being in stationary phase using phase-contrast microscopy (cells were large, with a single vacuole, and < 10% showed buds). The cells were then harvested, washed twice in sterile water, resuspended in water at a density of 1 × 108 cells/ml at t = 0, and then shaken aerobically (flask volume/medium volume, 5:1) at 37 °C. At the indicated time intervals, serial dilutions of these cell suspensions were prepared and plated on YPD agar plates, so that cell viability could be determined by colony counting.
Decapping assays
Unlabelled and uncapped RNA was produced by means of in vitro transcription using T7 polymerase (New England Biolabs). Plasmid pBS2266 digested with SmaI was used as a template, generating a transcript of 23 nt. The RNA was purified and cap-labelled using the vaccinia virus capping enzyme in the presence of [α-32P]GTP and S-adenosyl-methionine.8 Vaccinia capping enzyme large subunit43 was synthesized as a polyHis-tagged protein in E. coli and purified in two steps using Ni-resin and a heparin column. 32P-labelled cap dinucleotide was generated by treating the capped RNA with nuclease P1 (Roche), as described.3 32P-labelled m7GDP was produced by cleavage of capped mRNA using Dcp1/Dcp2 decapping activity that had been partially purified from a dcs1Δ strain by gel filtration. Unlabelled m7GpppG was purchased from New England Biolabs, while unlabelled m7GDP was from Sigma. The decapping assays were performed at 30 °C for the specified time periods in decapping buffer (10 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.0), 100 mM KOAc) using 0.5 pmol (300–1000 c.p.m.) of 32P-labelled substrate. Cell extract, prepared as described,44 or purified proteins from S. cerevisiae, were used in the assay. Reactions were stopped by extraction with phenol:chloroform (1:1) and with chloroform. Samples were spotted on PEI-cellulose TLC plates (Merck) and were run in 0.3–0.5 M LiCl, 1 M formic acid. TLC plates were dried and exposed to screens (Fuji) that were scanned with a Phosphoroimager and analysed using ImageQuant 5.1 (Molecular Dynamics). It was confirmed, using standards, that the TLC system discriminated reliably between the products m7Gp and Pi. Quantification of the gel spot radioactivities using a phosphorimager allowed us to construct plots of radioactivity in the respective species against dilution level (Supplementary Figure 4), and these in turn were used as the basis for constructing the bar plots shown in Figure 3.
Fluorescence microscopy
N-terminal green fluorescent protein (GFP)-fusion constructs were integrated into the chromosomal loci of DCS1 and DCS2. The resulting strains (PTC220 (GFP-DCS1), PTC221 (GFP-DCS2) and PTC222 (GFP-DCS1 in a dcs2Δ background)), as well as yRP1727 (DCP2-GFP) and yRP1729 (LSM1-GFP), were grown to different stages of growth. Further comparative data are shown in Supplementary Figure 3. Cells were washed in PBS buffer and applied on the slide together with DAPI in mounting medium. The preparations were analysed using an epifluorescence microscope (Zeiss) equipped with an HC Plan APO OS 100× oil NA 1.4 objective.
Immunoprecipitation
Synthesis of FLAG-tagged Dcs2 was directed from the plasmid pRS315-FLAG-DCS2 in the S. cerevisiae strain PTC143 (Y12429). Cells were grown in YPD medium containing 2% glucose to late log phase and washed in lysis buffer LB (50 mM Hepes (pH 7.5), 150 mM NaCl, 0.1% NP-40) including protease inhibitor cocktail. The cell pellet was resuspended in 1 ml of LB per gram of cells and lysed using glass beads. The cell extract was clarified by centrifugation at 14,000 rpm for 10 min in a microcentrifuge. Cleared extract (0.5 ml) was incubated with 50 μl of anti-FLAG-M2 affinity gel (Sigma-Aldrich) for 1 h at 4 °C, then washed three times with buffer LB and once with buffer LB without NP40. FLAG-tagged protein complexes were eluted twice for 10 min at room temperature in elution buffer (100 mM Hepes (pH 7.5), 100 mM NaCl) by competition with 3xFLAG peptide (Sigma). Eluates were separated by SDS-PAGE gel. Proteins were detected by Coomassie staining and Western blotting using anti-FLAG and anti-Dcs1 antibodies.
